output.summary: KEP-3157 proposes letting informers receive a stream of objects via a WATCH request (served from the watch cache) instead of a paginated LIST, so that LIST memory use becomes roughly constant per request. The KEP is currently implementable at stage beta.
output.rationale: LIST requests served from etcd allocate roughly O(5 * response size) of temporary memory, which can OOM kube-apiserver and its node. Streaming the initial state through the watch mechanism keeps per-request allocation bounded. Reviewers accepted the design, with concerns about watch-cache buffering and client-side enablement addressed in later discussion.

alternatives.option: Tune the priority and fairness cost function for LIST requests
alternatives.why_not: The cost of a LIST is hard to estimate because object sizes vary across the keyspace, and the estimate would be uniform over coarse dimensions, forcing the server to handle very few LISTs at a time.

alternatives.option: Measure real-time memory use and throttle when a threshold is exceeded
alternatives.why_not: runtime.ReadMemStats requires stop-the-world pauses and is too costly; reading /proc adds polling CPU cost and delay; cgroup notifications do not give free memory on the node.

alternatives.option: Serve paginated LISTs directly from the watch cache
alternatives.why_not: It would still allocate memory for the entire response, held until the client finishes receiving it (up to 60s), so the memory problem would not be solved.

alternatives.option: Force all clients to use pagination and let the server shrink page sizes
alternatives.why_not: Suggested by lavalamp as an alternative in discussion; the KEP does not record a reason it was rejected, and it is not the chosen design.

evidence.quote: The primary idea is to use standard WATCH request mechanics for getting a stream of individual objects, but to use it for LISTs. This would allow us to keep memory allocations constant.
The bottom line is around O(5*the_response_from_etcd) of temporary memory consumption.
it also presents a few challenges. The most concerning is that it would actually not solve the issue.
This design provides the ability for well-behaved clients to reduce the load they place on the server and improve their own deserialization memory cost.
